newsitem.title: UK: N Irish hopes still alive after Blair talks.
newsitem.headline: N Irish hopes still alive after Blair talks.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair appeared on Monday to have kept alive the chances of autumn negotiations on Northern Ireland's future at crucial talks with the leader of the province's largest Protestant party.

Blair met David Trimble of the Ulster Unionists, the main party representing the pro-British Protestant majority, to discuss worries that Britain had made concessions that persuaded the IRA to call a new ceasefire at the weekend.

While a smaller unionist party said it would boycott talks on Northern Ireland's future because Blair had softened demands for the IRA to "decommission" or scrap its arms, Trimble emerged from the meeting in a less combative mood.
"There are some possibilities of progress... but the matter is not yet clear," he told waiting reporters.
A Blair aide said later: "The important point from our point of view is that there was a clear desire on their (the Ulster Unionists') part not to walk out of the talks."

Parties to the peace talks must vote in Belfast on Wednesday whether to accept government proposals for guerrilla disarmament to be tackled in tandem with the discussion on Northern Ireland's constitutional future.
Trimble said unless the government clarified its position before Wednesday, his party would have to vote against.

"This, however, may not mean that the talks process ends. That depends on what the government and others do. We will not shirk our responsibilties. We are not in the mode of walking out. We are there to try to achieve things," Trimble later told a news conference.

He said he was seeking cast-iron assurances from the government that Irish Republican Army guerrillas would have to hand in some arms during the talks -- not after them -- and that they would face sanctions if they failed to do so.
Trimble said it was not even certain that the formula for disarming guerrillas would come to a vote this week.
"It is also possible that the issue will not come to a head on Wednesday," he said.
Just as the government had gone to great lengths to provide clarifications for Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, so it should do the same now for the Ulster Unionists, he added.
"It is not unreasonable to expect a similar period of time for consideration, for clarification, for exploration of the issues..." Trimble said.
He and Blair's aide both said there would be further contacts before Wednesday.
"While I am not going to pretend that there was an agreement, there was an agreement to try to carry on trying to understnad each others' difficulties," the Blair aide said.
